objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the reasons for an instrument flight deck check, teach a learner one systematic flow that covers all 17 items the PTS lists, describe how a defect in each item shows up from walk-around to takeoff roll, and decide with the learner whether the airplane can still go IFR under 91.205, 91.213 and the other rules.
why: Before any flight by instrument reference, the pilot should check all instruments and their sources of power; the check takes little time, but its importance cannot be overemphasized [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. The pilot in command decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]], and for IFR every item 91.205(d) lists must be in operable condition [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]] [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. Your job is to turn a list the learner recites into a habit of looking, comparing and deciding.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner finishes the run-up in under two minutes and reports "all instruments checked." You ask what the attitude indicator did in the last taxi turn and how far the heading indicator was from the runway heading at lineup. She does not know. What did she actually check, and how would you teach her a check that finds defects instead of reciting a list?

key_terms.def: The check of all instruments and their sources of power before any flight by instrument reference, done before start, after start, in taxi and before takeoff [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
With the current altimeter setting the altimeter should show field elevation; more than 75 feet off makes its accuracy questionable, and it should go to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
Shows the difference between the displayed heading and the magnetic heading of a slaved system; full deflection while turning is normal [[23:111|IFH 5-16]].
A mode of a remote indicating compass in which the card is not slaved and is set with the heading-drive buttons [[23:111|IFH 5-16]].
An FAA VOR test signal for checking a receiver on the ground: CDI centered at 0° FROM or 180° TO, and an RMI shows 180° [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. The limit is ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]].

Solid-state sensors that replace the separate attitude, heading and turn gyros [[23:117|IFH 5-22]]; it sets the horizon line at initialization, and the pilot cannot adjust the aircraft symbol [[23:155|IFH 6-22]].
The composite display a glass panel reverts to when one or more display screens fail [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].
Keeps the essential bus and PFD powered after the main battery is depleted on many glass panels; it must be armed before departure to work [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].
A TCAS II maneuver, climb or descend only, to avoid traffic; respond immediately unless unsafe, and tell ATC [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]].
Uses GPS position and a terrain and obstacle database to give aural and visual cautions and warnings based on time to impact [[23:129|IFH 5-34]] [[23:130|IFH 5-35]].

The FMS or GPS data of navaids, airways and procedures, updated every 28 days [[23:122|IFH 5-27]]. The AIM says it must be updated for IFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]; with an expired one, IFR use needs the data verified, and an approach not amended since the expiry date [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]].

Without an MEL, an inoperative item may stay only if it is not VFR-day type-certification equipment and no equipment list, KOEL, operating rule or AD requires it, it is removed or deactivated and placarded, and a pilot or mechanic decides it is no hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

chunks.title: The reasons for the check, and how this Task is tested

body.p: **The reasons for the check.** Inspecting the instrument system takes only a small part of the preflight, but its importance cannot be overemphasized. Before any flight by instrument reference, check all instruments and their sources of power for proper operation [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. It is critical that all systems are found operational before departing into IFR conditions [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

Three more reasons to give a learner. The pilot in command decides whether the airplane is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. For IFR, every 91.205(d) item must be in operable condition [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]] [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. And checking the directional instruments before taxi helps prevent runway incursions, because it keeps the pilot sure of the airplane's position relative to the runway and other traffic [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

**Know the power sources first.** Instruments are designed with redundancy so that a single failure does not leave the pilot unable to finish the flight, and gyros are powered by separate electrical or pneumatic sources [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. Have the learner find in the POH what powers each instrument [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. The check then becomes a check of each system, not just each dial.

body.p: **How this Task is tested.** The PTS objective is that you describe the reasons for the check and the detection of defects that could affect safe instrument flight, for all 17 items [[FAA-S-8081-9E:29|PTS III.C]]. In the PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating, Area III lists Task C in every column, and a Task listed there is mandatory [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Additional Rating Table]]. Parts of the Task may be done in a flight simulation training device, but an aircraft is required for the items a device cannot check [[FAA-S-8081-9E:50|PTS Appendix 1]].

callout.text: Application: open the lesson with a question, not a list: "What could hide a bad instrument from you in a cloud?" Then show that every item on the check answers that question for one system.

check.q: A learner asks why she has to look at the suction gauge when "the attitude indicator looks fine." What do you say?
check.a: The check covers the instruments and their sources of power [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. With low suction the attitude and heading indicators may be unreliable even if they look normal [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

chunks.title: Teaching a systematic check: one flow, said out loud

body.p: Teach the check as a flow the learner can repeat in any airplane, then tie it to that airplane's checklist. Checklists are the flight deck resource for verifying that instruments and systems are checked, set and working, and the more advanced the airplane, the more crucial they become [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]. The IFH steps fit conventional instruments; airplanes with electronic displays use the flight manual procedures [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: **Use demonstration-performance.** Explain the flow on the ground, demonstrate it, let the learner perform it while you supervise, then evaluate [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Learners imitate the instructor, so demonstrate the check exactly the way you want it practiced and in the same order you explained it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

**Watch for the recited checklist.** A verbal checklist can become so automatic that the words are decoupled from the thoughts and actions they should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]. Make the learner say the value she sees, not just the item: "altimeter 1,210, field 1,180, within 75 feet" is a check [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]; "altimeter set" is not.

callout.text: Application: when the learner finds a discrepancy, ask what resources could tell her whether it matters: her knowledge of the airplane, the POH, an instructor or an AMT [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]. Then ask what the rules say before she decides.

check.q: Your learner sets the heading indicator to the compass right after engine start. What do you correct?
check.a: Allow 5 minutes after start for the gyro to spin up, then set it before taxi or while taxiing straight [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: **Altimeter.** Set the current altimeter setting and check that the pointers show the airport elevation [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. If the indication is not within 75 feet of field elevation, its accuracy is questionable and it should be referred to a repair station. The ramp may be well above or below field elevation, so recheck in the run-up area before deciding. With no altimeter setting available, set the published field elevation [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

The records matter too. To fly IFR in controlled airspace, each static system, altimeter and automatic altitude reporting system must have been tested within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]], and no one may fly IFR in controlled airspace above the highest altitude to which they were tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]]. The altitude reporting equipment must have been tested and calibrated to report within 125 feet of the altimeter normally used to hold altitude [[60:495|14 CFR 91.217(a)(2)]].

**VSI.** It should read zero; if it does not, tap the panel gently [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. If it still shows a small climb or descent, use that reading as the zero mark, and expect it to trend upward after takeoff [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]].

**Airspeed indicator.** Before takeoff it should read zero, although a strong wind blowing straight into the pitot tube can make it read above zero. On the takeoff roll it should increase at an appropriate rate [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Errors in the airspeed indicator and VSI almost always mean a blocked pitot tube, static port or both, so the walk-around check of the pitot cover and static ports comes first [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].

On a later flight, cover the altimeter and ask what a static blockage would do to the other two static instruments.

check.q: On the ramp your learner's altimeter read 95 feet above field elevation with the current setting. At the run-up it still reads 90 feet high. What now?
check.a: Still more than 75 feet off after the recheck in the run-up area, so its accuracy is questionable and it should go to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. A sensitive altimeter is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(5)]], so the IFR flight waits.

chunks.title: Pitot heat, outside air temperature and the clock

body.p: **Pitot heat.** Check it by watching the ammeter when it is turned on, or by the method in the POH/AFM [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. The IFH sample IFR flight turns on the master switch and pitot heat and quickly checks the heating element before it becomes too hot [[23:322|IFH 10-31]]. The reason: the pitot tube is particularly vulnerable to icing, since even light icing can block the hole where ram air enters [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-11a]], and pitot heat is provided for flight in visible moisture [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

For operations in or near icing conditions, check the pitot heat, pitot tube opening and stall warning system on the preflight [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(4)]], and before takeoff verify that the airspeed indicator works and the pitot heat is on [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-6a]]. Pitot heat can also affect the magnetic compass, so it belongs on the list of equipment that causes deviation [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]].

**Outside air temperature.** The OAT gauge is a simple bimetallic thermometer with its sensing element in the outside air, and an accurate reading tells the pilot how temperature changes with altitude [[1:230|PHAK 8-28]]. Ice forms when there is moisture and the air is 0 °C or colder, and aerodynamic cooling can form ice even when the air is slightly above freezing [[23:314|IFH 10-23]]. That is why the IFH says to monitor the OAT whenever the airplane is in visible moisture [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]. On glass panels the ADC uses the OAT probe to compute the true airspeed shown on the airspeed tape [[1:214|PHAK 8-12]].

Two OAT traps to teach. A heated probe on some aircraft can be clogged by ice crystals; the reading then rises to 0 °C and holds [[38:30|AC 91-74B 3-11f]]. And for cold-temperature altimeter corrections, use the reported temperature at the station, not the temperature at the airplane's altitude [[23:101|IFH 5-6]].

**Clock.** IFR requires a clock showing hours, minutes and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(6)]]. Before start it should be set to the correct time and running [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. The learner needs it for timed turns with the turn coordinator [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] and for finding the missed approach point by timing from the FAF when the navaid is away from the airport [[23:40|IFH 1-21]], using the chart's time and speed table [[23:46|IFH 1-27]].

callout.text: Application: compare the ramp OAT with the ATIS or AWOS temperature, and start the clock's timer on the runway as part of the lineup flow. No source here gives a tolerance for either check, so teach "does it make sense?"

A clock without seconds, or one that has stopped, does not meet 91.205(d)(6) [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(6)]], and an item 91.205 requires cannot be deferred for that kind of flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

check.q: Your learner's pitot heat check shows no change on the ammeter. The forecast is IMC in rain with temperatures above freezing. What do you discuss?
check.a: The check failed [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Pitot heat is not on the 91.205 list [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], so whether it can be deferred depends on the equipment list, KOEL, ADs and 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. Even if legal, even light icing can block the pitot [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-11a]], so ask where the freezing level is and how she would get out of the moisture.

body.p: **Before start**, the compass should be full of fluid and the correction card in place and current. **After start**, check that the card moves freely and the bowl is full, then compare the indicated heading with a known heading, such as the runway heading, while stopped or taxiing straight. Remote indicating compasses are checked against known headings too. Note the card correction for the takeoff runway heading [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

Why it matters: in most small airplanes the magnetic compass is the only direction-indicating instrument independent of other airplane instruments and power sources [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The heading indicator is set from it [[23:115|IFH 5-20]], and it is required for every flight, VFR or IFR [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(3)]] [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(1)]].

body.p: Precipitation static can also cause erroneous compass readings in flight, one reason broken or missing static wicks should be replaced before an instrument flight [[23:328|IFH 11-3]].

callout.text: Application: on the runway centerline, have the learner read the runway number, the compass with its card correction and the heading indicator in one breath. The AFH asks that the runway numbers agree with the compass and heading indicator before the takeoff roll [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

check.q: After start your learner finds the compass 12° off the runway heading with the radios on, and the card shows a 2° correction. What do you teach?
check.a: Compare it while stopped or taxiing straight and apply the card correction [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. It is still about 10° off. First rule out interference from radios, pitot heat or deice [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]]. No source here sets a limit, but an error the card does not explain needs an AMT, since only AMTs adjust the compass or complete the card [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]], and the compass is required for every flight [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(3)]].

body.p: **Heading indicator.** Allow 5 minutes after engine start for the gyro to spin up, then set it to the magnetic compass before taxiing or while taxiing straight [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Before takeoff, recheck it: with an accurate compass and deviation card it should show the known taxiway or runway direction within 5° [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. In taxi turns it should turn the correct way with normal precession; at idle, vacuum gyros may not be up to speed, so precession can be faster than in flight [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]].

A free gyro drifts. Earth's rotation alone gives an apparent drift of up to 15° per hour, so it is compared with the compass at least every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]] [[1:222|PHAK 8-20]]. Worn, dirty or poorly lubricated bearings can make the drift excessive [[1:222|PHAK 8-20]].

**HSI and slaved systems.** A slaved gyrocompass is checked for slaving action and compared with the magnetic compass [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. In most HSIs the compass card is driven by a flux valve, and the HSI has a compass warning flag and a NAV warning flag [[23:118|IFH 5-23]]. The slaving meter shows the difference between the displayed heading and the magnetic heading. Full deflection while turning is normal, and in free gyro mode the card is set with the heading-drive buttons [[23:111|IFH 5-16]].

**RMI.** The compass card is driven by the flux valve and shows the heading under the upper index; the two pointers are driven by the ADF and the VOR receiver [[23:111|IFH 5-16]]. Tuned to a VOT, an RMI shows 180° on any OBS setting [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]].

callout.text: A gyroscopic direction indicator (directional gyro or equivalent) is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(9)]]. An inoperative one cannot be deferred for an IFR flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

check.q: Lined up on runway 27, the heading indicator reads 281° while the compass, corrected, reads 270°. What do you tell your learner?
check.a: It should show the runway direction within 5° [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. Reset it to the compass and watch it; if it drifts off again quickly, worn or dirty bearings may be causing excessive drift [[1:222|PHAK 8-20]], and it should be fixed before an IFR flight.

body.p: **Attitude indicator.** When the master switch goes on, listen to the gyros spin up; any hesitation or unusual noise should be investigated before flight. Then check their power source: suction for vacuum gyros, generators and inverters for electric ones [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. A typical vacuum reading is 4.8 to 5.2 inches of mercury at 2,000 rpm, but use the POH value [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

The gyro normally erects in 2 to 3 minutes and can take up to 5 [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. It is working if the horizon bar erects and stays at the correct position for the airplane's attitude, or vibrates and then slowly stops [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. If the bar does not stay horizontal in straight taxi, or tips more than 5° in taxi turns, the instrument is unreliable. Set the miniature aircraft to the horizon bar on the ground [[23:133|IFH 5-38]], and look for warning flags [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

A hasty taxi and run-up does not give mechanical gyros time to spool up, and a departure into IMC that way is unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. If an electronic flight instrument system is installed, check the emergency attitude system, including its battery [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

**Turn coordinator.** Before start, the miniature aircraft should be level and the ball about centered on level ground [[23:132|IFH 5-37]], and the inclinometer should be full of fluid with no air bubbles [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. In taxi turns it should show the turn in the correct direction, with the ball moving freely and opposite the turn; in straight taxi the miniature aircraft should be level [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. It shows rate and direction of turn, not bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]], and it does not sense pitch [[23:117|IFH 5-22]]. An older **turn-and-slip indicator** shows only rate of turn; the canted turn coordinator first shows roll rate, then rate of turn. Both show turn direction and coordination [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]], so the same taxi check applies: correct turn direction, ball free and opposite the turn [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

Most airplanes have at least two sources of power so that at least one source of bank information remains if one fails, and the turn instruments serve as that backup when an attitude indicator fails [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. That is why the turn coordinator check is not a formality.

callout.text: IFR requires a gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator (unless the airplane has a third attitude instrument system installed under 121.305(j)), a slip-skid indicator and a gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. None of them can be deferred for an IFR flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

check.q: In each taxi turn the attitude indicator banks about 10° and comes back slowly. Suction is in the green. What do you tell your learner?
check.a: Tipping more than 5° in taxi turns makes it unreliable [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. A gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]], so this flight does not go IFR until it is fixed.

body.p: **The checks.** On the walk-around, check the condition of all antennas [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. Radio switches stay off for engine start; after start, check the radios for proper operation and set them [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Broken or missing static wicks should be replaced before an instrument flight, because precipitation static can cause a complete loss of VHF communications [[23:328|IFH 11-3]].

**Why.** IFR requires two-way radio communication equipment suitable for the route [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(2)]]. Each IFR flight should still be planned as if a two-way radio failure could happen [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. On a day VFR flight a single radio is not a major concern, but in IMC having one radio could be an "A" hazard [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

**Transponder and ADS-B.** The transponder must have been tested within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]], and in controlled airspace an operable transponder must be on, with Mode C if installed [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. The ADS-B Flight ID must match the aircraft identification in the flight plan, or ATC may not link the airplane to its flight plan [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7]]. Transponder and ADS-B should be on whenever the airplane is in the air or on the airport surface movement area [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner copy the ATIS on one radio and the clearance on the other, and say which radio is for what. Beginning instrument learners often mix up two comm radios with active and standby frequencies; error rates drop quickly once they understand each radio's purpose [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

Under IFR in controlled airspace, report any in-flight malfunction of navigation, approach or communication equipment to ATC as soon as practical, with the equipment affected, how it impairs IFR operation, and the help needed [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

check.q: Your learner hears the ATIS clearly on COM 1, but ground control says her transmissions on COM 2 are unreadable. She says one good radio is enough. How do you guide her decision?
check.a: IFR needs two-way radio equipment suitable for the route [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(2)]], and in IMC a single radio can be an "A" hazard [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Ask whether one radio and her lost-communication plan fit the weather and route [[23:333|IFH 11-8]], and how the bad radio will be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

body.p: **Before the flight.** Navigation equipment must be suitable for the route to be flown [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(2)]]. Check the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs for the condition and frequencies of the navaids you will use; the IFH still calls it the A/FD [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

**VOR.** To use VOR under IFR, the equipment must be maintained under an approved procedure or checked within the preceding 30 days and found within limits [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. The limits are ±4° with a VOT or repair-station test signal or at a designated ground checkpoint, both at the airport of intended departure, and ±6° at an airborne checkpoint, used only when neither is available [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]]; with dual VORs, 4° between the two [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. Log the date, place, bearing error and a signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. With a larger error, IFR flight must not be attempted until the source of the error is corrected [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

Teach the traps. Apply no correction other than the manufacturer's correction card [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]. Some propeller rpm settings make the CDI fluctuate as much as ±6°, and a slight rpm change usually smooths it. Never use a VOR reading taken while transmitting. For sensitivity, moving the CDI from center to the last dot should take no more than 10° or 12° of OBS either side [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. A receiver can pass close to a VOT and still be out of tolerance far from a station, so yearly calibration is recommended [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

**GPS.** IFR GPS must be an approved, properly installed unit; VFR and hand-held units are not authorized for IFR navigation [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. With un-augmented GPS the airplane needs another approved, working means of navigation for the route, such as VOR. If RAIM is predicted to be unavailable, use other approved equipment, reroute, delay or cancel [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. Review GPS NOTAMs before any GPS IFR operation, and if the GPS becomes inoperative, advise ATC and amend the equipment suffix [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

callout.text: VOR: 30 days. VOT ±4°, ground ±4°, airborne ±6°, dual 4° apart. Log date, place, error, signature [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

check.q: At the VOT your learner centers the CDI with the OBS at 355° and a FROM flag. Can she use the VOR for IFR?
check.a: A perfect check is 0° FROM [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]], so 355° is a 5° error, beyond the ±4° VOT limit [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. IFR using that VOR must wait until the error is corrected [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

body.p: **Use the flight manual.** The IFH preflight steps are for conventional instruments; airplanes with electronic flight instrument systems use the flight manual procedures [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. For the practical test, any flight instrument display using LCD or picture-tube-like screens is an "electronic flight instrument display"; general aviation airplanes typically have a PFD and an MFD [[23:122|IFH 5-27]].

**What to check.** The IFH's electronic items: check the emergency instruments and the emergency system, including its battery [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. On many glass panels the standby battery must be in ARM to work, and arming should be done before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. The AHRS sets the horizon line at initialization, and there is no need or means for the pilot to adjust the aircraft symbol [[23:155|IFH 6-22]]. The AFH taxi checks of attitude, altimeter, turn indication, heading and VSI apply to glass displays as well [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

**How defects show.** An AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading indications from the PFD, and all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold are lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. When a display fails, the system reverts to a composite (reversionary) mode [[23:329|IFH 11-4]], since the PFD and MFD can each show the critical information [[23:123|IFH 5-28]]. In the IFH's example airplane, the standby instruments are an attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator and magnetic compass [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

**Why it matters.** Glass displays depend on the electrical system for the AHRS, ADC and engine indications, so an alternator failure that is an abnormality in a round-dial airplane is an emergency in a technically advanced one [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. Pilots also tend to drop the standby instruments and the compass from the scan; they must keep monitoring them to detect failures [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

callout.text: The electronic display is a supplementary source of navigation data and does not replace en route charts; if the screens fail, the pilot who relied only on the moving map loses position, nearest airport and traffic awareness [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

check.q: On start-up the PFD shows ATTITUDE FAIL and it does not clear. Your learner suggests flying the standby attitude indicator. What do you say?
check.a: In the IFH, ATTITUDE FAIL is the AHRS failure display [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]: the PFD has lost attitude and heading and most autopilot modes [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. Standby instruments like those in the IFH example give attitude, airspeed and altitude, with only the magnetic compass for heading [[23:331|IFH 11-6]], and a gyroscopic direction indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(9)]]. No IFR today.

body.p: **What it is.** An FMS combines a database of navaids, airways, intersections, SIDs, STARs and approach procedures with pilot inputs through a control display unit to build the flight plan. It sends course guidance to the HSI and roll steering to the autopilot and flight director. Navigation databases are updated every 28 days [[23:122|IFH 5-27]].

**The check.** At system initialization, confirm the database is current and includes the procedures you need, and verify that the airplane's position is correct [[40:43|AC 90-105A A.7.1.2]]. Find the issue date and make sure the planned use is before the expiration date, and check that the provider has not published a notice limiting a waypoint or procedure [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. The AIM says databases must be updated for IFR operations [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]], and approaches must be retrieved by name from the database, not entered as waypoints [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. Its GPS table is more precise: with an expired database, en route and terminal use needs the data verified for correctness, and an approach needs a current database or proof that the procedure has not been amended since the expiry date [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]].

**Then check the programming.** Before departure, verify everything programmed on the ground, compare the route with a paper log, verify waypoints, and use VOR and GPS to back each other up [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. Make sure the waypoint sequence matches the ATC route and the chart at the first clearance and after every change [[40:43|AC 90-105A A.7.1.3]].

callout.text: If the database will expire during the flight, plan how to verify the data. For a U.S. approach, if the procedure amendment date is on or after the database expiry date, do not fly that procedure with the old database [[40:43|AC 90-105A A.7.1.2]].

check.q: Your learner's GPS database expired yesterday. She plans an RNAV approach at the destination. What do you teach?
check.a: The preflight check is that the planned use is before the expiration date [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]], so update it before the flight. If she cannot, the approach may be flown only if it has not been amended since the database expired [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]]; one amended on or after the expiry date must not be flown with it [[40:43|AC 90-105A A.7.1.2]].

body.p: **Traffic.** TCAS I issues traffic advisories to help the pilot see the intruder [[23:125|IFH 5-30]]; TCAS II adds resolution advisories [[23:129|IFH 5-34]]. On a TA, try to see the traffic but do not deviate from a clearance on the TA alone. On an RA, respond immediately unless that would be unsafe or the crew can ensure separation by seeing the traffic, and tell ATC about any deviation [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]]. An operable TCAS must be on and operating [[60:498|14 CFR 91.221(b)]].

Smaller airplanes often use a traffic alert system as a cost-effective alternative to TCAS [[23:125|IFH 5-30]], or an ADS-B In traffic display [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. These give no avoidance guidance: an ADS-B traffic display must not be used for avoidance maneuvers in IMC [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7]], TIS-B shows only transponder-equipped targets and needs radar coverage [[33:305|AIM 4-5-8]], and TCAS does not respond to aircraft without a working transponder [[33:288|AIM 4-4-16]]. A clear traffic screen does not mean a clear sky.

**Terrain.** GPWS uses the radio altimeter and gives only limited prediction of rising terrain, and none in mountainous areas. TAWS uses GPS position and a terrain and obstacle database to give aural and visual warnings [[23:129|IFH 5-34]], and its cautions and warnings are based on time to impact rather than distance [[23:130|IFH 5-35]]. TAWS is required for turbine-powered airplanes with six or more passenger seats, and the AFM must contain procedures for its use and for the crew's reaction to its warnings [[60:498|14 CFR 91.223]].

**Detecting defects.** The rule sends the pilot to the AFM for TAWS procedures [[60:498|14 CFR 91.223(c)]], and the PHAK suggests using the MFD terrain page for night or IMC flight near mountains [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. Application: teach the learner to find the self-test and the failure annunciations in the AFM supplement, and to plan the flight as if the system were not there when the test fails.

callout.text: AFMs prohibit using the moving map, terrain, traffic and weather datalink displays as the primary data source [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].

check.q: In cloud, your learner's ADS-B In display shows traffic 2 miles ahead at her altitude. She wants to turn away. What do you teach?
check.a: ADS-B traffic is advisory and must not be used for avoidance maneuvers in IMC [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7]]. Ask ATC. Only a TCAS II RA is a maneuver you follow without visual contact [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]].

body.p: **What it is.** An autopilot keeps the airplane in level flight or on a set course and can be coupled to a radio navigation signal. It has a disconnect safety feature, can be manually overridden, and is operated as the AFM/POH describes [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]. Most general aviation autopilots control roll and pitch [[23:120|IFH 5-25]]. A flight director only gives steering commands that the pilot, or a coupled autopilot, follows [[23:119|IFH 5-24]].

**The check.** Before engaging, accomplish the flight director and autopilot computer and trim checks; many newer systems will not engage without a completed self-test. Know the normal and emergency ways to disengage; details and limitations are in the AFM/POH supplements [[24:257|AFH 13-8]]. Set the autopilot preselects during the run-up [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

**How defects show.** Know at all times which modes are engaged and which are armed, and confirm armed modes engage when they should. With some autopilots, changing the navigation source in NAV mode drops lateral control to ROL until the pilot re-engages NAV [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. A failing vacuum gyro connected to the autopilot or flight director can cause incorrect movement [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

**Go or no-go.** 91.205 does not list an autopilot [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], but an inoperative one known before departure should factor into the other risks, for example a night approach to minimums the pilot planned to fly coupled [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]. Flying IMC without an autopilot raises workload and can be treated as an "A" hazard [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Where an RNP approach needs the autopilot or flight director, they must be installed and working [[40:44|AC 90-105A A.7.1.6]].

callout.text: Unless the AFM/POH says otherwise, the autopilot should not be used in icing: it masks the trim changes that warn of ice and can disconnect suddenly at its limits [[24:259|AFH 13-10]].

check.q: During the run-up test, the autopilot will not disconnect with the control wheel button. What now?
check.a: The pilot must know the normal and emergency disengagement methods, and the AFM supplement holds the procedures and limitations [[24:257|AFH 13-8]]. Do not use it. If no equipment list, KOEL or AD requires it, it may be deferred: deactivated and placarded, with a no-hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]], and weigh the extra workload of IMC without it [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

chunks.title: A defect found: can the airplane still go IFR?

body.p: When the learner finds an inoperative item before departure, the choices are to cancel, get maintenance, or defer it legally. Deferral is not for in-flight discrepancies; those use the POH/AFM procedures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. With an approved MEL and a letter of authorization, the MEL governs [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]. A non-turbine airplane without an MEL uses 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]]:

bullets: 1. The item is not part of the VFR-day type certification equipment [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(i)]].
2. It is not required by the equipment list or the KOEL for this kind of flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]].
3. It is not required by 91.205 or another Part 91 rule for this flight, so nothing in 91.205(d) for IFR [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].
4. It is not required by an AD [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iv)]].
5. It is removed with the control placarded and the maintenance recorded, or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative" [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].
6. An appropriately rated pilot or mechanic decides it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

body.p: Legal is not the end of it. Deferral is not to be taken lightly; consider the effect of the item on the flight, especially when other items are also inoperative [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Any inoperative equipment is an "A" hazard to weigh against the expected conditions [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. An item that cannot be deferred and cannot be fixed on the field may be flown to a repair shop only under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

callout.text: Items can fail after takeoff. The pilot in command must discontinue the flight when an unairworthy condition occurs [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]], and under IFR in controlled airspace must report navigation, approach or communication malfunctions to ATC as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]].

Application: give the learner a placard and a scenario card for each defect and have her walk the six 91.213(d) questions aloud, then the risk question. Examiners often ask "Can we go?" right after "What would you see?"

check.q: No MEL. The VSI is cracked and reads nothing. It is not VFR-day type-certification equipment, the equipment list and KOEL do not require it, and there is no AD. What does the learner need before an IFR flight?
check.a: The VSI is not on the 91.205 list [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], so it can be deferred: removed or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative," with any maintenance done and recorded under Part 43, and a determination that it is no hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

scenario.title: Early IFR departure in the club Archer
scenario.setup: Your instrument learner is three weeks from her checkride and plans a 7 a.m. IFR departure in the club's Piper Archer: a six-pack with a vacuum-driven attitude and heading indicator, an electric turn coordinator, one VOR receiver, an IFR-approved WAAS GPS navigator and a two-axis autopilot. The airplane has no MEL. The ceiling is 800 overcast with tops near 5,000 feet, and the freezing level is 9,000 feet. The departure airport has a VOT. The last VOR check in the logbook was 33 days ago, and she plans a VOR approach at her alternate.

questions.q: She says the VOR check does not matter because she will fly GPS. How do you respond?
questions.a: She plans to use the VOR under IFR at the alternate, so it must have been checked within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. With a VOT on the field the fix takes a minute: CDI centered at 0° FROM or 180° TO, within ±4°, then log date, place, bearing error and signature [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

questions.q: Right after start she sets the heading indicator and reaches for the brakes to taxi. What do you say?
questions.a: Allow 5 minutes for the gyro to spin up, then set it before taxi or while taxiing straight [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Have her recheck it against the runway heading at lineup, within 5° [[23:133|IFH 5-38]].

questions.q: At the run-up the suction gauge reads below the green arc at 2,000 rpm. The gyros look normal. Can they go?
questions.a: With low suction the attitude and heading indicators may become unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]; use the POH range [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Both instruments are required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]] and cannot be deferred for it [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]], so not into an 800-foot overcast.

questions.q: Another day the vacuum is fine, but the pitot heat check shows no change on the ammeter. Can she go?
questions.a: Pitot heat is not on the 91.205 list [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], so check the equipment list, KOEL and ADs, and defer it properly if allowed [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. The cloud is well below the freezing level, but aerodynamic cooling can form ice slightly above freezing [[23:314|IFH 10-23]], so have her monitor the OAT in the clouds [[23:327|IFH 11-2]] and know her way out.

questions.q: The autopilot then fails its preflight test. What do you weigh?
questions.a: 91.205 does not require it [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]], so if the equipment list, KOEL and ADs allow, it can be deferred: deactivated and placarded [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]]. An autopilot known to be inoperative before departure should factor into the other risks [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]], and IMC without one raises workload [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. With you aboard, it can be good checkride practice.

questions.q: How do you debrief the check so the next one is better?
questions.a: Have her assess herself first, then compare it with your assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. Ask why each miss happened and what she will do differently next time [[25:85|AIH 3-34]], and have her rebuild her flow from the IFH phases [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

skills.do: At the airplane, explain aloud how you check the attitude indicator and turn coordinator from master switch to takeoff roll: what you listen and look for, what a good and a bad indication look like, and whether the airplane can go IFR with each defect.
skills.practice: Sit in the airplane with another applicant as your learner and run the IFH sequence in order, naming each limit: 5 minutes to spin up, no more than 5° in taxi turns, ball opposite the turn [[23:132|IFH 5-37]] [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. Have your partner invent a defect at each step and answer with the rule [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

skills.do: Brief a glass-panel flight deck check as you would to a learner: the AFM flow, standby instruments and standby battery, AHRS start-up, database and programming checks, and what each failure display means for IFR.
skills.practice: Walk through your airplane's AFM supplement on the ground [[23:131|IFH 5-36]], adding standby battery arming [[23:331|IFH 11-6]], the database date and route check [[40:43|AC 90-105A A.7.1.2]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]], and an explanation of reversionary mode [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

quiz.q: On the ramp, with the current setting, your learner's altimeter reads 85 feet above field elevation. What should she do first?
options: Recheck it in the run-up area before deciding
Set field elevation in the window and depart
Accept it, since the IFR limit is 100 feet
Placard it inoperative and plan to fly VFR only today
quiz.why: The ramp may be well above or below field elevation, so when the error is more than 75 feet, recheck in the run-up area; if it is still more than 75 feet off, refer it to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Setting field elevation is only for when no altimeter setting is available, and no source gives a 100-foot limit.

quiz.q: Lined up on runway 09 with an accurate compass and card, your learner's heading indicator reads 098°. What does the IFH say?
options: Fine: up to 10° is normal before the gyro settles
Fine: 15° per hour of drift is normal on the ground
Too far off: it should be within 5° of the runway
Fine: reset it after takeoff when the compass is steady
quiz.why: Before takeoff the heading indicator should show the known runway direction within 5° [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. The 15° per hour figure is the apparent drift from Earth's rotation, the reason to compare with the compass every 15 minutes, not a ground tolerance [[23:115|IFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: In each taxi turn the attitude indicator banks about 8° and returns slowly. What do you teach?
options: Normal, because taxi turns are uncoordinated
Unreliable: it may tip 5° at most in turns
Normal until the gyro has run for 30 minutes
Adjust the miniature airplane and then recheck
quiz.why: If the horizon bar tips more than 5° in taxi turns, the instrument is unreliable [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. Adjusting the miniature aircraft only sets the level reference; it does not fix tipping. A gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]].

quiz.q: How should your learner check the magnetic compass after engine start?
options: Swing it on the compass rose and update the card
Compare it with the heading indicator in a taxi turn
Leave it alone until airborne, once the engine is fully warm
Against a known heading, stopped or taxiing straight
quiz.why: Check that the card moves freely and the bowl is full, then compare it with a known heading such as the runway heading while stopped or taxiing straight [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Swinging the compass and filling in the card are AMT tasks [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]].

quiz.q: At the VOT your learner centers the CDI and the OBS reads 182° with a TO flag. What is the result?
options: A 2° error, within the ±4° VOT limit
A 2° error, outside the ±1° VOT limit
No result: a VOT is only read with FROM
A 182° error: the receiver has failed
quiz.why: With the CDI centered, a VOT should give 0° FROM or 180° TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. 182° TO is 2° off, and the limit with a VOT is ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. The ±1° figure is the course alignment accuracy of a VOR station, not the check limit [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

quiz.q: Your airplane has two independent VOR receivers. Tuned to the same station they show 211° and 216°. What do you tell your learner?
options: Fine: the dual-receiver check allows up to 6°
Fine, as long as she flies the lower reading
Not within limits: the maximum is 4° apart
Fine: average the two and use 213° instead
quiz.why: With dual VORs, the maximum variation between the two indicated bearings is 4° [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]. 6° is the airborne checkpoint limit [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]], and no correction other than the manufacturer's card should be applied [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

quiz.q: Before departure in this glass-panel airplane, your learner leaves the upper switch in OFF. What is the problem?
options: None: the standby battery comes on by itself
The standby battery must be armed to work
The master switch will not stay in ON now
The alternator will not charge the battery
quiz.why: The standby battery comes online when the main battery is depleted to about 19 volts, generally only if its switch is in ARM, and arming should be done before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

quiz.q: In IMC with a TCAS I, your learner gets a traffic advisory for traffic 600 feet below. What should she do?
options: Climb at once to gain more vertical separation
Turn away from the target shown on the display
Descend, since TCAS I shows the safe direction
Look for it and keep to her ATC clearance
quiz.why: TCAS I gives proximity warning only, and no avoidance maneuvers are provided or authorized from a TCAS I warning. On a TA, try to see the traffic but do not deviate from the clearance on the TA alone [[33:287|AIM 4-4-16]].

quiz.q: Which of these does 91.205 NOT require for IFR?
options: Vertical speed indicator
Slip-skid indicator
Clock showing seconds
Generator or alternator
quiz.why: 91.205(d) lists the slip-skid indicator, a clock with hours, minutes and seconds, and a generator or alternator of adequate capacity, but no VSI [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. The IFH also notes the VSI is not required for instrument flight [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

quiz.q: No MEL. The ADF is inoperative; it is not type-certification equipment, no equipment list, KOEL or AD requires it, and the route does not need it. What else is needed before an IFR flight?
options: Nothing: a radio that is not needed can be ignored
A special flight permit from the FSDO for the flight
Remove or deactivate it, placard it, judge it no hazard
A written note on the clipboard for the mechanic to read later
quiz.why: The item must be removed or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative," and a pilot or mechanic must decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]]. A special flight permit is for an airplane that cannot otherwise be operated, to fly it to repair [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

quiz.q: Your learner tunes the VOR to the VOT. On this RMI, which pointer does she check, and what should it show?
options: Green pointer: 360° with the OBS set to 000
Yellow pointer: 180° on any OBS setting
Green pointer: 180° on any OBS setting
Yellow pointer: the OBS setting plus 180°
quiz.why: In this RMI the yellow pointer is driven by the VOR receiver and the green one by the ADF [[23:111|IFH 5-16]]. On a VOT an RMI indicates 180° on any OBS setting [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]].

quiz.q: The club airplane's panel clock shows hours and minutes but no seconds. Can it be flown IFR?
options: Yes, if the learner carries a phone timer
Yes, the clock is required only for night
Yes, if it is placarded as inoperative
No: IFR needs hours, minutes and seconds
quiz.why: IFR requires a clock displaying hours, minutes and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(6)]]. An item 91.205 requires for the flight cannot be deferred with a placard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

quiz.q: Coupled in NAV on GPS, your learner switches the CDI source to LOC for the approach. The autopilot annunciates ROL. What happened?
options: The autopilot failed and must be turned off
The localizer is too weak to capture just yet
Changing the nav source dropped the NAV mode
The flight director has taken over steering
quiz.why: With some autopilots, changing the navigation source while in NAV mode disengages NAV, and lateral control defaults to ROL until the pilot re-engages NAV [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. That is why the learner must always know which modes are engaged and armed [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

final_quiz.q: Which preflight check of the pitot heat does the IFH give?
options: Hold the tube with a bare hand for one full minute
Watch the ammeter as it comes on, or use the POH
Make sure the pitot heat breaker is pushed in
Look for a green PITOT HEAT light on the annunciator
final_quiz.why: Check the pitot heater by watching the ammeter when it is turned on, or by the POH/AFM method [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. The IFH sample flight checks the element quickly, before it becomes too hot [[23:322|IFH 10-31]], so a long hold is wrong.

final_quiz.q: In cloud the OAT reads +2 °C. Your learner says ice is impossible above freezing. What do you teach?
options: She is right: ice forms only below -10 °C
She is right, as long as pitot heat is on
Ice needs freezing rain, and none is reported
Aerodynamic cooling can form ice above 0 °C
final_quiz.why: Aerodynamic cooling can lower an airfoil's surface temperature and form ice even when the air is slightly above freezing [[23:314|IFH 10-23]]. Pilots should monitor the OAT in visible moisture [[23:327|IFH 11-2]] and be vigilant between -5 °C and +2 °C [[38:13|AC 91-74B 2-1d]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's database expired two days ago. The RNAV approach she plans was amended after that expiry date. What do you say?
options: Do not fly that approach with the old database
Fly it; only the en route part of the data must be current
Fly it if the waypoint names match the chart
Fly it if RAIM is predicted to be available
final_quiz.why: If the procedure amendment date is on or after the database expiry date, the procedure should not be flown with the out-of-date database [[40:43|AC 90-105A A.7.1.2]]. With an expired database, an approach needs proof that it has not been amended since the expiry date [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]]; matching names and RAIM do not make old data current.

final_quiz.q: The ADS-B Flight ID in your learner's avionics does not match the aircraft identification on her IFR flight plan. What can happen?
options: Nothing: ATC uses only the transponder code
Her traffic display will stop showing other targets
ATC may not link her to her filed flight plan
The transponder will switch itself to standby mode
final_quiz.why: The Flight ID must match the aircraft identification in the flight plan; if it does not, ATC automation may not associate the aircraft with its flight plan, and services may be delayed or unavailable [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner finds that the transponder was last tested 25 calendar months ago. What does the rule say?
options: It may still be used, but not in Class A airspace
It may not be used until it is tested again
It may be used under VFR with Mode C off
It may be used if ATC approves each flight
final_quiz.why: No one may use an ATC transponder unless it was tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]], regardless of airspace [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: The altimeters and encoder were last tested to 12,000 feet. Your learner files IFR at 14,000 feet in controlled airspace. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, if the test was within 24 months
She must set 29.92 above 12,000 feet
Only the encoder must be tested that high
IFR above the tested altitude is not allowed
final_quiz.why: No one may fly IFR in controlled airspace above the maximum altitude to which all altimeters and the altitude reporting system have been tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]]. Being within 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]] does not remove that limit.

final_quiz.q: On a glass panel the AHRS fails on the ground. What does the PFD lose?
options: Attitude, heading and most autopilot modes
Airspeed and altitude, but not the attitude
Only the heading, since the AHRS is a compass
Nothing, because the ADC backs up the AHRS
final_quiz.why: An AHRS failure removes all attitude and heading indications from the PFD, and all autopilot modes except roll and altitude hold are lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. Airspeed and altitude come from the ADC [[23:117|IFH 5-22]] [[23:118|IFH 5-23]].

final_quiz.q: Taxiing in an airplane with a slaved HSI, the slaving meter swings full scale in each turn and centers on straight taxiways. What does this mean?
options: The flux valve failed; switch to free gyro mode
The card is 30° off; reset it with the buttons
Normal: the meter deflects fully while turning
The HSI gyro has not finished spinning up yet
final_quiz.why: The slaving meter shows the difference between displayed and magnetic heading, and whenever the aircraft is turning and the card rotates, it shows full deflection to one side [[23:111|IFH 5-16]]. Centering in straight taxi is what you want.

final_quiz.q: On the walk-around your learner notices two static wicks missing. Why does it matter for an IFR flight in rain?
options: They hold the static ports open in rain
Precipitation static can kill VHF radios
91.205 requires them for every IFR flight
They heat the antennas so ice cannot form
final_quiz.why: Precipitation static can cause erroneous compass readings and complete loss of VHF communications; broken or missing static wicks should be replaced before an instrument flight [[23:328|IFH 11-3]].

final_quiz.q: When the master switch goes on, your learner hears a gyro whine, hesitate and grind. What should happen?
options: Nothing: gyros are noisy until up to speed
Wait 5 minutes and see if the noise stops
Note it for the next annual inspection
Investigate it before flight, as the IFH says
final_quiz.why: Listen to the gyros as they spin up; any hesitation or unusual noise should be investigated before flight [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. The PHAK check also says to make sure there are no abnormal sounds as the gyro spools up [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's IFR GPS has no WAAS (TSO-C129). What else must the airplane have for an IFR route?
options: Another approved, working means of navigation
A hand-held GPS unit as the second navigation source
Nothing else, if RAIM is predicted available
A second GPS receiver of the very same model
final_quiz.why: Aircraft using un-augmented GPS under IFR must have an alternate approved and operational means of navigation suitable for the route, such as VOR or DME/DME/IRU; VFR and hand-held GPS are not authorized for IFR navigation [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. RAIM availability removes only the need to actively monitor the alternate equipment [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner wants to update the compass correction card herself after noticing new deviation. What do you say?
options: Fine, if she logs it as preventive maintenance
Fine, if she uses the airport compass rose
No: only an AMT may adjust it or fill in the card
Fine, if the change is less than 5 degrees
final_quiz.why: Only AMTs can adjust the compass or complete the compass correction card; pilots fly the headings the card gives [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]].

final_quiz.q: What does a TAWS base its cautions and warnings on?
options: Radio altimeter height above the ground only
GPS position, terrain data and time to impact
ATC radar returns sent to it by the ADS-B uplink
Distance to the nearest charted obstacle, nothing else
final_quiz.why: TAWS uses GPS positioning and a database of terrain and obstructions [[23:129|IFH 5-34]], and gives warnings and cautions based on time to potential impact rather than distance [[23:130|IFH 5-35]]. The radio altimeter is the basis of the older GPWS [[23:129|IFH 5-34]].

final_quiz.q: In IMC under IFR in controlled airspace, your learner's VOR receiver fails. What must her 91.187 report to ATC include?
options: Only the aircraft identification and position
The time of failure and the last radial flown
Nothing until landing, as long as GPS works
Equipment, effect on IFR and help she wants
final_quiz.why: The report must include the aircraft identification, the equipment affected, the degree to which IFR capability is impaired, and the nature and extent of assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]], made as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner rattles off "instruments checked" in five seconds. Which AIH idea explains your concern?
options: A recited checklist can be decoupled from action
Overlearning always makes a checklist safer
Speed shows she has fully mastered the check
Rote recall is the highest level of learning
final_quiz.why: A verbal checklist can become so automatic that the recitation is decoupled from the thoughts and actions it should trigger, and the pilot may not stop to consider each item [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

final_quiz.q: In a glass-panel airplane, which instruments does the IFH say pilots tend to leave out of the scan?
options: The airspeed and altitude tapes
The attitude display and the HSI
The standby instruments and compass
The trend vectors on the tapes
final_quiz.why: Because the PFD is so reliable, pilots tend to omit the standby instruments and the magnetic compass from their scans, and they should keep monitoring them to detect failures [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

takeaways: Check the instruments and their power sources before any IFR flight; the pilot in command decides airworthiness.
Teach one flow: walk-around, before start, after start, taxi, run-up, takeoff roll. Make the learner say values, not item names.
Numbers: altimeter within 75 feet, gyros 5 minutes, heading indicator within 5° at lineup, attitude indicator no more than 5° in taxi turns.
VOR: 30 days; VOT and ground ±4°, airborne ±6°, dual 4°; log date, place, error and signature.
Glass: follow the AFM, arm the standby battery, check the standby instruments, the database and the programming.
Traffic and terrain displays are advisory; only a TCAS II RA is flown without seeing the traffic, and TAWS procedures are in the AFM.
Anything 91.205 requires cannot be deferred; everything else goes through 91.213(d) and then a risk decision.
cfi_notes: Suction values differ by source: the PHAK says usually 4.5 to 5.5 "Hg [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]], the AFH typically 4.8 to 5.2 "Hg at 2,000 rpm [[24:59|AFH 2-22]], and the IFH venturi example about 4 "Hg for the attitude instruments [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. Teach the POH range for the airplane.

Two IFH wordings to correct: its preflight list still says Airport/Facility Directory [[23:131|IFH 5-36]], now the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]]; and IFH 9-16 says the VOR check needs "an appropriate endorsement" [[23:259|IFH 9-16]], while the rule requires a log entry with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. Teach the current name and the rule.

PHAK 9-10 says deactivation may be as simple as the pilot positioning a circuit breaker to OFF, and that complex deactivation needs a certificated, appropriately rated maintenance person [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]; the rule says deactivation that involves maintenance must be done and recorded under Part 43 [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]]. Neither says exactly where that line falls, and AC 91-67A, which covers it, is not one of these sources; agree with your maintenance shop how your school deactivates items.

The IFH says the ball should move opposite the direction of taxi turns [[23:132|IFH 5-37]] and the AFH says toward the outside of the turn [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]; they describe the same thing. Pick one phrase for the learner.

The IFH flow is written for conventional instruments and sends glass-panel pilots to the flight manual [[23:131|IFH 5-36]], while the AFH says its taxi instrument checks work on either [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Teach both: the AFM flow, then the taxi cross-check.

The PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating lists Area III Task C in every column [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Additional Rating Table]], and the objective verb is "describing" [[FAA-S-8081-9E:29|PTS III.C]]. Expect "What would you see if...?" followed by "Can we go?" for items the examiner picks, often in the test airplane.

The IFH GPWS and TAWS text uses airline and transport examples [[23:129|IFH 5-34]] [[23:130|IFH 5-35]]; 91.223 requires TAWS only in turbine-powered airplanes with six or more passenger seats [[60:498|14 CFR 91.223(a)]]. For a light airplane, the AFM supplement for the installed unit is the real reference.

Who may compensate the compass: IFH 5-13 says "the pilot or AMT" aligns the airplane and adjusts the compensating magnets [[23:108|IFH 5-13]], while PHAK 8-25 says only AMTs can adjust the compass or complete the correction card [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]]. Teach the PHAK: the pilot may taxi the airplane onto the compass rose headings, the AMT adjusts and fills in the card.

Expired databases: AIM 1-1-17 says databases must be updated for IFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]], but its GPS table allows en route and terminal use with verified data, and approaches not amended since the expiry date [[33:101|AIM 1-1-17]], as does AC 90-105A for U.S. approaches [[40:43|AC 90-105A A.7.1.2]]. Teach "update it" as the habit and the amendment-date check as the exception.
gaps: No source here gives a tolerance for the OAT gauge, or a test for the clock beyond "set to the correct time and running" [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
No source here gives a limit for magnetic compass error against the runway heading, or for slaving meter error on the ground.

Airplane-specific procedures, such as suction range, EFIS start-up, standby battery test, autopilot and TAWS or traffic self-tests, come from the AFM/POH and its supplements [[24:257|AFH 13-8]], which are not in these sources.
AC 91-67A (MEL, KOEL and deactivation practice) is not a build source; the deferral rules here come from 14 CFR 91.213 and PHAK 9-9 to 9-10.
No source here says whether pitot heat is required for a given Part 91 airplane under IFR; that depends on its equipment list, KOEL and icing approval.

activities.title: Put the flow in order
activities.intro: Put the instrument checks in the order the learner does them, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Walk-around and records: antennas, pitot and static ports, 24-month check
Before start: radios off, altimeter set, clock running
Master on: listen to the gyros spin up
Check suction or the electrical source for the gyros
After 5 minutes, set the heading indicator to the compass
Taxi turns: turn coordinator, ball, heading and attitude indicators
Lineup: heading indicator within 5° of the runway
Takeoff roll: airspeed rising at an appropriate rate
activities.why: Sequence from the IFH systems preflight procedures [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[23:132|IFH 5-37]] [[23:133|IFH 5-38]] and the PHAK airspeed check on the takeoff roll [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

activities.title: What you see, what it means
activities.intro: Tap what the learner sees, then what it means.

pairs.l: Altimeter 90 ft off field elevation, also at the run-up
pairs.r: Accuracy questionable: send it to a repair station

pairs.l: VSI shows 100 fpm down on the ramp
pairs.r: Use that reading as the zero mark

pairs.l: Airspeed reads above zero, parked in a strong wind
pairs.r: Wind blowing into the pitot tube

pairs.l: Airspeed stays at zero on the takeoff roll
pairs.r: Pitot blockage: stop and find the cause

pairs.l: Altimeter frozen and VSI at zero after a climb
Altimeter slightly high, airspeed high, VSI a brief climb

activities.title: Where does 91.205 put it?
activities.intro: Tap an item, then the part of 91.205 that lists it for an IFR flight.
buckets: Day VFR list (b), so also IFR
activities.why: From [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]] and [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. Items not on the list still need a proper 91.213(d) deferral if inoperative [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

activities.title: Work the check numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: VOT check: the CDI centers with the OBS at 357° and a FROM flag. What is the bearing error in degrees?
items.why: A perfect VOT check is 0° FROM [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]; 360 - 357 = 3°, within the ±4° limit [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]].

items.q: Dual VOR check to the same station: 093° and 097°. How many degrees apart are they?
items.why: 97 - 93 = 4°, exactly the maximum permitted between the two [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

items.q: Field elevation 1,180 ft. With the current setting the altimeter reads 1,265 ft. How many feet off is it?
items.why: 1,265 - 1,180 = 85 ft, more than 75 ft, so recheck in the run-up area and, if still off, refer it to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

items.q: A free heading indicator has not been reset for 40 minutes. Up to how many degrees of apparent drift can Earth's rotation alone cause?
Standard-rate timed turn: how many seconds for a 45° heading change?
items.why: Standard rate is 3° per second: 45 / 3 = 15 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

activities.title: Read the glass panel
activities.intro: Tap the indication, then what it means.

pairs.l: ATTITUDE FAIL on the PFD after start
pairs.r: AHRS failed: no attitude or heading on the PFD

pairs.l: PFD screen blank, flight instruments on the MFD
pairs.r: Reversionary mode after a display failure
The standby battery will not work if needed

pairs.l: Alternator failure in a glass-panel airplane
pairs.r: An emergency: shed load, land as soon as practical

pairs.l: Autopilot shows ROL after a CDI source change
Standby attitude and compass never in the scan

activities.title: True or false: radios and navigation
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A VOR check at a designated ground checkpoint may be off by up to 6°.
cards.why: False. The ground checkpoint limit is ±4°; ±6° is for an airborne checkpoint [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]].

cards.s: The VOR check record needs the date, place, bearing error and a signature.
Some propeller rpm settings can make the CDI swing as much as ±6°.
cards.why: True. A slight rpm change usually smooths it [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

cards.s: A hand-held GPS with a current database is approved for IFR navigation.
cards.why: False. VFR and hand-held GPS systems are not authorized for IFR navigation [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: If the GPS becomes inoperative, advise ATC and amend the equipment suffix.
Missing static wicks can lead to a loss of VHF communications in precipitation.
cards.why: True. Precipitation static can cause complete loss of VHF communications [[23:328|IFH 11-3]].

cards.s: The 24-month transponder test applies only to flight in Class A airspace.
cards.why: False. It applies to using the transponder regardless of airspace [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]] [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

cards.s: Electronic navigation databases are updated every 28 days.

activities.title: How a TAWS warns
activities.intro: Drag each label to the frame of the TAWS sequence it describes.

pins.label: The real terrain ahead of the airplane
Terrain painted the way the TAWS shows it
Terrain display and alert panel in the flight deck
Caution: terrain to be crossed ahead
Warning: aural and red PULL UP, pilot climbs

activities.why: Frames from IFH Figure 5-59: A shows the airplane and the outside terrain, B and C how the TAWS displays the terrain, D a caution, E a warning with aural and red text and the pilot climbing, and F the hazard no longer a factor [[23:130|IFH 5-35]].

activities.title: One morning, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFII for an instrument learner flying the club's round-dial trainer, with no MEL, into a 900-foot overcast. Each step is a separate find; make the call.

steps.s: Logbook: the VOR check was 35 days ago. The field has a VOT, and the alternate plan is a VOR approach.
options: Skip it: she will fly GPS for the whole trip anyway
Do the VOT check, within ±4°, and log it
Use the old check, since 35 days is close enough
Do an airborne check after takeoff in the clouds
steps.why: VOR used under IFR needs a check within 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. With a VOT at the departure airport, use it (±4°) and log it [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]; an airborne checkpoint is only for when no test signal or ground checkpoint is available [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]].

steps.s: After start the suction gauge reads below the green arc at 2,000 rpm. The gyros look normal.
options: Go: the gyros look normal, so they are fine
Add rpm until the needle is green, then go
No IFR: the gyros may be unstable and inaccurate
Go, but plan to fly partial panel from takeoff
steps.why: When vacuum drops below the normal range, the gyro instruments may become unstable and inaccurate [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]], and the AFH value is given at 2,000 rpm [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. The attitude and heading indicators are required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

steps.s: Taxiing out, the attitude indicator tips about 8° in each turn.
options: Normal for taxi turns; it will settle in flight
Unreliable: no IFR until it is fixed
Fine if the turn coordinator works normally
Re-cage it at the run-up, then go if level
steps.why: Tipping more than 5° in taxi turns makes it unreliable [[23:133|IFH 5-38]], and a gyroscopic pitch and bank indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]].

steps.s: At lineup on runway 18, the heading indicator reads 183° and the corrected compass agrees with the runway.
options: Reject: any difference means a bad gyro
Go: it is within 5° of the runway heading
Reset the compass card to match the gyro
Taxi back and swing the compass first
steps.why: The heading indicator should show the runway direction within 5° [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]; 3° is within it. Only an AMT adjusts the compass or its card [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]].

steps.s: Climbing through 3,000 feet in cloud, COM 1 fails. COM 2 works.
options: Say nothing, since one radio still works
Squawk 7600 at once and stop talking
Report it to ATC on COM 2 as soon as practical
Wait until on the ground to report it
steps.why: Under IFR in controlled airspace, communication equipment malfunctions in flight are reported to ATC as soon as practical, with the equipment affected, the effect on IFR and the help needed [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. Two-way communication still works, so this is not a lost-communications case.
